---
title: "Ground Truth"
---

::: {.ao-story}
A script glows in the maze and claims to have been tested, and the companion that wrote it swears it works. It sounds sure of itself, and its light shows nothing new. A traveller carries a lantern of their own: a measurement the script did not make. Light it and see whether the script is telling the truth.
:::

::: {.quest-dialog}
- **Goal:** you will find out whether a script an agent called "tested" is right, using a check the agent did not write. You need this before you rely on any agent-written code.
- **Before you start:** [Spot Hallucinations](spot-the-mirage.html), a terminal with Python 3 and `awk`, and the two files below (about 1 KB in total). Nothing here touches your own data.
- **Time:** about 15 minutes.
:::

Files: [tiny.fasta](../../exercises/maze/tiny.fasta) (three short DNA sequences in FASTA, a text format where each `>` line names a sequence) and [gc.py](../../exercises/maze/gc.py). Save both into an empty folder.

## Check the script with an independent count

An agent gave you `gc.py`, which reports the GC content of each sequence (the percentage of its bases that are G or C), and said "tested, works". Run it yourself:

```bash
python gc.py tiny.fasta
```

You should see:

```
seq1	50.0
seq2	20.0
seq3	25.0
```

Now measure the same thing a different way, with a tool the agent did not write. This `awk` command uppercases each line, counts G and C, and counts the total length:

```bash
awk '/^>/{if(n)print n"\t"gc" GC of "t" total"; n=substr($1,2); gc=0; t=0; next}
     {s=toupper($0); t+=length(s); gc+=gsub(/[GC]/,"",s)}
     END{print n"\t"gc" GC of "t" total"}' tiny.fasta
```

```
seq1	6 GC of 12 total
seq2	6 GC of 10 total
seq3	2 GC of 8 total
```

Work out the percentages and compare them row by row with the script. One row differs: seq2. The seq3 row matches because both methods count the Ns in the total; whether they should is a decision, not a bug. Then take the battle.

## Say what the agent did

When agent work reaches a paper or a report, a few habits keep it traceable:

- **Cite by persistent identifier:** a permanent ID, such as a DOI for a paper or an accession number for a dataset. Confirm that the identifier points to the real source.
- **Generate references with a tool that is not a language model,** so a model does not write the reference text. Keep retraction status with the citation.
- **Separate person from agent:** make clear what a person did and what an agent did, and disclose agent use where results are published. Check your target journal's own rules.
- **Record each run:** the model version, the inputs and the tool calls, so you can look again later. This record of where a result came from is called provenance.
- **Stay accountable:** the judgement is yours whatever the agent found.

## Lore

*Further reading. Optional.*

- [Best practices for Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices): Anthropic, docs. Why read: it says to give the agent a way to check its work; this quest's check is one the agent did not write.
- [AI for Science, practice 7: provenance and citation](https://aiforscience.eu/best-practices/07-provenance-and-citation/): AI for Science (European draft best practices), docs. Why read: it covers citing by identifier, generating references with a deterministic tool, and disclosing agent use. A draft; it calls one of its own cited papers self-audited.
- [Reduce hallucinations](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations): Anthropic, docs. Why read: it lists model-side habits (quote first, retract unsupported claims); read it to see why a check the model did not write is still needed.
- [The Strawberry Problem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.14172): arXiv (EMNLP 2025), paper. Why read: it studies why models miscount letters and links it to tokens, which is the idea behind miscounted bases.
- [Counting Ability of LLMs and Impact of Tokenization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.19730): arXiv, paper. Why read: it shows how tokenisation changes counting accuracy in language models, which is why a script, not a model's reading, should do exact counts (that last step is our general practice, not the paper's claim). A preprint.
:::
